messages.subject: Point transect density estimates
parts:
All,

I have a few questions regarding estimating passerine density at the poin=
t
transect scale. I'm new to distance sampling, but have been reading about=
it
and working with the program for over a year.=20

Our research goal is to identify relationships between passerine bird
densities and habitat characteristics. I plan find these relationships vi=
a
multiple linear regression.=20

Here is the sample design:

- 101, 100-m radius point transect plots, established within shrub-steppe=

habitat of Colorado
- Surveyed during breeding season in two years (2006 and 2007), visited e=
ach
point transect two times per year (one observer, same observer for all fo=
ur
visits)
- Passerine birds detected by sound, distances recorded to nearest 10 m f=
or
each detected bird
- Habitat characteristics (cover, shrub density, vegetation structure)
measured in each point transect

Data structure in Distance (pooled data):

Study area - Label =3D BrownsPark, Visits =3D 4 (used as a Multiplier, ac=
tually
a divider)=20
Region - Label =3D 1, Area =3D 0=20
Point Transect - Label =3D 1 thru 101, Survey Effort =3D 1=20
Observation - Radial Distance =3D 10 - 100 m, Species =3D four letter spe=
cies code

My purpose for using Program Distance (v5.0, r2) is to estimate a detecti=
on
function for each of the most common species (detections > 60), upon whic=
h
will be used to adjust the raw counts for an estimate of density (both at=

study site and point scale).=20

I've had no problems with data import or running analyses. I'm using the
Conventional Distance Sampling engine. I've followed the suggested
instructions from Intro to Distance Sampling (Buckland et al 2001), the
Distance User's Manual/Help and Distance-Sampling List Archives as there =
are
few people on my campus that are well versed in Distance.=20

My questions (1-2) center on the estimates of density (D), probability of=

detection (p), and probability detection function slope (h(0)) that Dista=
nce
provides. So far I've only worked with the most abundant species from the=

data set, Brewer's Sparrow (BRSP). Results from modeling pooled BRSP data=

are listed at the end of this message. I selected the hazard-rate key wit=
h
simple polynomial adjustment detection function based on lowest AICc.

1. It was recently suggested to me to re-calculate D, as the one provided=
by
the program is inaccurate. Is this true? And is it also true of p and h(0=
)?
I re-calculated D for BRSP, and the estimates are slightly different (whi=
ch
is probably due to rounding). I'm wondering if I should re-calculate the
estimates, and if so, am I using the correct equation for D (see below).

For example...

Brewer's Sparrow, n =3D 284 (pooled across years, 10 10m intervals, 80m
truncation)
h(0) =3D 0.18073E-02=20=20
p =3D 0.17291=20=20=20=20
c =3D 4

CDS global density estimate =3D 202.21 birds/km2 Re-calculated global den=
sity
estimate =3D 202.31 birds/km2
=09(D-hat =3D n*h(0)-hat/c*2*pi*k, eqns 3.15 and 3.69, Intro book)

2. For an estimate of density at the point scale, do I use the global
detection function parameters, including p and h(0)? I know this question=

has been posted several times on the list, but it is still unclear. I was=

able to get point (sample) density estimates for BRSP from Distance (CDS)=

('Estimate' tab, 'Quantities to estimate...Sample - Density and Encounter=

Rate, Global - Detection Function'). I know there are a few issues with t=
his
procedure (lack of independence and accounting for variation). Despite th=
is,
are the density estimates for each point reported in the analysis results=

correct? Or do I need to calculate an average p and h(0) for point
estimates? I ask this because I recently read on calculating average
probability of detection in Chapter 8 and am a bit confused (not about th=
e
procedure but on whether or not to use the global estimate of p from Dist=
ance).

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Point transect density estimates
parts:
Mary, I'm not sure why your adviser would believe that we would program
Distance to be inaccurate! Of course you don't have to recalculate
estimates of density! I'm sure you're right that the small difference
you found was because you were using rounded values output from Distance.

Note however that Distance rounds estimates of N to the nearest
integer. This doesn't generally make much difference, but will if you
estimate abundance for each point (or at least a circle around each
point). You should probably instead work with the estimated density at
each point.

Using a global detection function is OK if you believe that
detectability is the same at each point. Failing that, if you have
recorded say habitat covariates at each point, you can use the MCDS
engine to fit a single detection function model to all data, but to
allow detectability vary according to habitat. If you assume that
detectability doesn't vary, then you could simply model the counts
themselves to assess how habitat affects numbers. I suspect that this
is not plausible though!

You may want to take a look at chapter 4 of the advanced distance
sampling book (2004), which considers how to model point transect data
when densities vary by habitat. We're also currently working on a paper
outlining how to model counts when detectability varies - hopefully this
will be ready for submission to a journal very soon. I'll send you a
draft off the list.

Steve Buckland

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Point transect density estimates
parts:
Mary, I'm not sure why your adviser would believe that we would program
Distance to be inaccurate! Of course you don't have to recalculate
estimates of density! I'm sure you're right that the small difference
you found was because you were using rounded values output from Distance.

Note however that Distance rounds estimates of N to the nearest
integer. This doesn't generally make much difference, but will if you
estimate abundance for each point (or at least a circle around each
point). You should probably instead work with the estimated density at
each point.

Using a global detection function is OK if you believe that
detectability is the same at each point. Failing that, if you have
recorded say habitat covariates at each point, you can use the MCDS
engine to fit a single detection function model to all data, but to
allow detectability vary according to habitat. If you assume that
detectability doesn't vary, then you could simply model the counts
themselves to assess how habitat affects numbers. I suspect that this
is not plausible though!

You may want to take a look at chapter 4 of the advanced distance
sampling book (2004), which considers how to model point transect data
when densities vary by habitat. We're also currently working on a paper
outlining how to model counts when detectability varies - hopefully this
will be ready for submission to a journal very soon. I'll send you a
draft off the list.

Steve Buckland

Mary Williams wrote:

> > All,
> >
> > I have a few questions regarding estimating passerine density at the point
> > transect scale. I'm new to distance sampling, but have been reading about it

> > and working with the program for over a year.
> >
> > Our research goal is to identify relationships between passerine bird

> > densities and habitat characteristics. I plan find these relationships via
> > multiple linear regression.

> >
> > Here is the sample design:
> >
> > - 101, 100-m radius point transect plots, established within shrub-steppe

> > habitat of Colorado
> > - Surveyed during breeding season in two years (2006 and 2007), visited each
> > point transect two times per year (one observer, same observer for all four
> > visits)
> > - Passerine birds detected by sound, distances recorded to nearest 10 m for

> > each detected bird
> > - Habitat characteristics (cover, shrub density, vegetation structure)
> > measured in each point transect
> >
> > Data structure in Distance (pooled data):
> >

> > Study area - Label = BrownsPark, Visits = 4 (used as a Multiplier, actually
> > a divider)
> > Region - Label = 1, Area = 0
> > Point Transect - Label = 1 thru 101, Survey Effort = 1
> > Observation - Radial Distance = 10 - 100 m, Species = four letter species code
> >
> > My purpose for using Program Distance (v5.0, r2) is to estimate a detection
> > function for each of the most common species (detections > 60), upon which
> > will be used to adjust the raw counts for an estimate of density (both at
> > study site and point scale).
> >

> > I've had no problems with data import or running analyses. I'm using the
> > Conventional Distance Sampling engine. I've followed the suggested
> > instructions from Intro to Distance Sampling (Buckland et al 2001), the
> > Distance User's Manual/Help and Distance-Sampling List Archives as there are

> > few people on my campus that are well versed in Distance.
> >
> > My questions (1-2) center on the estimates of density (D), probability of
> > detection (p), and probability detection function slope (h(0)) that Distance
> > provides. So far I've only worked with the most abundant species from the
> > data set, Brewer's Sparrow (BRSP). Results from modeling pooled BRSP data
> > are listed at the end of this message. I selected the hazard-rate key with

> > simple polynomial adjustment detection function based on lowest AICc.
> >

> > 1. It was recently suggested to me to re-calculate D, as the one provided by
> > the program is inaccurate. Is this true? And is it also true of p and h(0)?
> > I re-calculated D for BRSP, and the estimates are slightly different (which

> > is probably due to rounding). I'm wondering if I should re-calculate the
> > estimates, and if so, am I using the correct equation for D (see below).
> >
> > For example...
> >

> > Brewer's Sparrow, n = 284 (pooled across years, 10 10m intervals, 80m
> > truncation)

> > h(0) = 0.18073E-02
> > p = 0.17291
> > c = 4
> >
> > CDS global density estimate = 202.21 birds/km2 Re-calculated global density
> > estimate = 202.31 birds/km2
> > (D-hat = n*h(0)-hat/c*2*pi*k, eqns 3.15 and 3.69, Intro book)

> >
> > 2. For an estimate of density at the point scale, do I use the global
> > detection function parameters, including p and h(0)? I know this question
> > has been posted several times on the list, but it is still unclear. I was
> > able to get point (sample) density estimates for BRSP from Distance (CDS)
> > ('Estimate' tab, 'Quantities to estimate...Sample - Density and Encounter

> > Rate, Global - Detection Function'). I know there are a few issues with this
> > procedure (lack of independence and accounting for variation). Despite this,
> > are the density estimates for each point reported in the analysis results

> > correct? Or do I need to calculate an average p and h(0) for point
> > estimates? I ask this because I recently read on calculating average

> > probability of detection in Chapter 8 and am a bit confused (not about the
> > procedure but on whether or not to use the global estimate of p from Distance).

> > For example...
> >
> > BRSP CDS point density estimate:

> > Sample(Point ID) : 2
> > Effort : 1.000000
> > Width : 80.00000
> > Left : 10.00000

> > # observations: 4

> > Model 1

> > Point ID 2, # BRSP = 4

> >
> >
> >
> > The density estimates seem a little high, but are similar to estimates

> >
